content: The pooled estimate of the drug regimen's effects carries less weight due to certain limitations. However, the direction and magnitude of the estimated effects, along with their confidence intervals, strongly support the presence of a drug effect. Despite both studies being randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the overall GRADE quality of evidence for the outcomes was rated as low, primarily due to the risk of bias in the underlying studies and imprecision in the estimates, particularly because of the small sample size in the Thomsen 2016 study. When comparing the combination of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine (DEC), and albendazole (IDA) to DEC with albendazole (DA) in non-onchocerciasis co-endemic areas, unpublished safety data from ongoing studies were analyzed. These studies included participants over five years old, weighing at least 15 kilograms, regardless of infection status, and accounted for the cluster design of the study. The pooled data from four countries showed no significant difference in adverse events between the intervention and control groups, with wide confidence intervals. However, fewer adverse events were observed in the intervention group, except in Haiti. For grade 3 and 4 adverse events, the small number of subjects introduced substantial uncertainty in both individual and pooled estimates. Serious adverse events (grade 4) were reported in only three cases in Haiti, making it challenging to estimate adjusted effects across all countries. The GRADE quality of evidence was rated as low due to the risk of bias in study designs and imprecision. A single study (Bjerum 2016) compared IDA to DA in non-onchocerciasis co-endemic areas, reporting outcomes such as microfilarial (MF) clearance, microfilarial density, and adult worm nest clearance. The intervention arm showed greater clearance and reduced microfilarial density, with statistical significance only for microfilarial density. The GRADE quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low due to high risk of bias and imprecision. Two studies (Kar 2015 and Kar 2016) compared biannual DEC with albendazole (DA) to annual DA in non-onchocerciasis co-endemic areas, reporting outcomes at 24 months. The estimates for microfilarial density showed no effect in one study and favored the control group in the other. Worm nest clearance estimates favored the intervention group but included a confidence interval crossing 1. The GRADE quality of evidence was rated as very low due to observational study designs, baseline differences, and serious imprecision. An observational study in Indonesia reported outcomes at 36 months, comparing biannual DA to annual DA. Microfilarial prevalence decreased in all communities, with a larger reduction in the intervention group, though the confidence interval was wide and included the null value. The GRADE quality of evidence was rated as very low due to the observational nature of the study, baseline differences, and imprecision. One RCT (Tafataha 2015) and two observational studies (DOLF Liberia and DOLF Côte d’Ivoire) compared biannual ivermectin with albendazole (IA) to annual IA in onchocerciasis co-endemic areas. The results for MF and circulating filarial antigen (CFA) prevalence changes were inconsistent, with reductions slightly higher in intervention communities in Liberia but favoring control communities in Côte d’Ivoire. The GRADE quality of evidence was rated as very low due to high risk of bias and imprecision. A single-arm cohort study (Pion) evaluated biannual albendazole in loiasis co-endemic areas, showing reductions in microfilarial density at three years. However, the GRADE quality of evidence was rated as very low due to the study design and imprecision. In summary, the systematic review included 14 studies published between 2004 and 2016, with most conducted in lowand middle-income countries. The studies had methodological limitations, including poor reporting of context, sampling, and methods. Community knowledge about lymphatic filariasis (LF) and mass drug administration (MDA) programs was generally low, with misconceptions persisting even after MDA campaigns. Positive community perceptions of MDA were associated with understanding the program's benefits and goals, while negative perceptions were linked to mistrust, fear of side effects, and suspicion about the program's motives. Participation in MDA campaigns was higher when communities were involved in planning and implementation, LF was considered a priority, and drug distributors were trusted.
